title: Miriam's tambourine (Exodus 15:19–21)
hook: Miriam takes a tambourine and the women dance and sing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sea: chariots behind, water ahead, and Moses saying stand still and see. Where did you stand still before you stepped forward? Day three hundred eighty-nine.

Here's a question nobody asks in the movie version. When the Israelites left Egypt in the middle of the night, with dough on their shoulders and no time to pack, who brought the tambourines? Someone did. Someone, grabbing what mattered in the dark, made room for a drum. On the far shore, with the sea closed behind them, Moses leads the people in a long song of victory. Then the text turns to someone else. A woman we may have met before, standing in the reeds watching a basket. Now she's old. And she's holding a hand drum.

In the King James Bible: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances." A timbrel is a hand drum, a frame drum, the tof in Hebrew. Miriam is the first woman in the Bible called a prophetess. And she doesn't just play. She leads, and she calls the song: "Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea." It's almost exactly the first line of Moses's song, turned into a call to everyone else. Many scholars think this short song may be among the oldest poetry in the whole Bible. Some even wonder whether Miriam's two lines came first, and the longer song grew from them. The text doesn't say, and we can't know. Exodus doesn't name the sister by the river, but tradition has long said it was Miriam. If so, the girl who watched her baby brother float in the reeds is the woman who leads the dancing on the other side of the water. There is also a hard side to the song, and Jewish teachers saw it. The Talmud tells of angels in heaven wanting to sing as the Egyptians drowned, and God stopping them: the work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing? Israel's song is thanks for rescue, not joy at anyone's death. Christians have sung Exodus fifteen for centuries; it's one of the canticles in many churches' morning prayer. Music, it turns out, was one of the things worth carrying out of Egypt.
screen: `MIRIAM THE PROPHETESS.` · `TIMBRELS AND DANCES.` · `THE GIRL BY THE RIVER, NOW OLD.` · `THANKS, NOT JOY AT DEATH.` · then, large: `SING YE TO THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: dance or tap a rhythm in thanks. Think of one thing you've been brought through: an illness, a bad year, a dangerous moment, a long wait that ended. Now give it a beat. Tap your hand on your knee, or the table, or your chest. Slow at first. Let it grow, the way Miriam's drum drew the women after her. Stand and sway if you like. If you pray, you can let the rhythm be your thanks to God. If you don't, let it be thanks anyway. The bell holds the time.
Miriam's tambourine. The hand drum Miriam the prophetess played on the far shore of the sea, leading the women in dance and song.
Your line: sing to the lord. Today, put on one song that lifts you, and let yourself move a little, even in the kitchen. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Many churches sing the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) as a canticle at morning prayer or the Easter Vigil, and in many Christian communities around the world praise with drums and dancing is a regular part of worship.

options: let the men's song be enough.
lead the women out with drums and dances, and sing.

fork.reveal: she takes up the timbrel, and all the women go out after her: "Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously."

original.note: Hebrew: a hand drum or frame drum, the timbrel Miriam played.

trapdoor: what you thought: Miriam played a tambourine at a victory party.
what it means: a prophetess leads the women in thanks for rescue, and later Jewish teachers insisted it was never joy at the enemy's death.
what a scholar hears: many scholars count the Song of Miriam among the oldest poetry in the Bible; some suggest it is the seed of the longer Song of Moses.

notes: The Talmud passage (Megillah 10b / Sanhedrin 39b) is paraphrased; confirm wording and citation.
Miriam as 'the first woman in the Bible called a prophetess' (15:20). Confirm.
'Now she's old': by Exodus chronology Moses is about eighty (Exodus 7:7) and Miriam older; the text does not give her age. Confirm the phrasing.
Scholarly views on the antiquity of Exodus 15 and the priority of Miriam's song are presented as views, not facts.
The Song of the Sea as a canticle (e.g. 'Cantemus Domino' in Lauds, Anglican and Lutheran usage). Confirm.
